This work establishes a new rare‐earth‐mediated strategy to frustrate deep reconstruction and stabilize a real active surface for efficient and stable hydrogen production.

title: Conjugation‐Activity Regulated Molecular Templates Enable Microcrystallite‐Refined Hard Carbon for High‐Performance Sodium Storage
abstract: ABSTRACT The microcrystallite structure of carbon materials has a significant impact on their electrochemical properties, yet it usually suffers from uncontrollable aromatic ordering and thickening during carbonization. Here, we develop a conjugation‐activity regulated molecular template strategy to program the microcrystallite evolution of coal‐derived hard carbon toward sodium storage. By modulating conjugation capacity and bond–cleavage thresholds of aromatic N‐heterocycles, we propose a molecular template design principle: strong conjugation creates supplementary microcrystallite growth sites to alter aromatic domain evolution, while molecular activity controls the effective activation range for conjugation‐mediated reconstruction. N‐Phenylcarbazole, which integrates a sufficiently conjugated aromatic core with a locally labile N‐phenyl linkage, realizes this balance by enabling radical‐mediated precursor reconstruction during pre‐oxidation and constrained aromatic‐layer rearrangement during carbonization. The resulting hard carbon exhibits refined and dispersed turbostratic microcrystallites with enlarged interlayer spacing and regulated defects, retaining 250.3 mAh g −1 after 5600 cycles at 500 mA g −1 , corresponding to 83.6% capacity retention. This work establishes an activity‐window‐modulated conjugated‐molecule design principle for programming coal‐derived carbon microcrystallites.

title: A Dicationic Diradicaloid through Intramolecular One‐Electron Transfer from a B‐B σ‐Bond to an Aromatic π‐System
abstract: ABSTRACT Herein we report on a novel type of main group diradicaloid with the triplet state arising from unprecedented reversible intramolecular one‐electron transfer from a B‐B σ‐bond (HOMO) into a boron‐bound organic π‐acceptor orbital (LUMO of pyrazine). The deep‐red bis(diboranyl)pyrazine dication, with a bridging pyrazine between two diboranyl units and sp 3 ‐hybridised boron atoms, represents also the first example for a fully‐reversible thermal redox equilibrium between a diborane as electron donor and an organic π‐acceptor. The compound is stable in solution and in the solid state under ambient conditions. Two modified systems were synthesised, demonstrating that a decrease of the B‐B σ‐bond orbital energy as well as an increase of the π*‐acceptor orbital energy leads to an extinction of the diradicaloid character.

title: Spin‐Selective Hydrogen Utilization Enables Efficient Electrochemical CO 2 ‐to‐CH 4 Conversion in Ag‐Modified Chiral Cu Catalysts for Unassisted Solar Fuel Production
abstract: ABSTRACT Although electrochemical CO 2 ‐to‐CH 4 conversion offers a viable pathway to sustainable fuel synthesis, its efficiency is limited by the difficulty of balancing the availability of reactive hydrogen species for multistep CO 2 hydrogenation against the suppression of the competing hydrogen evolution reaction (HER). Here, we establish a spin‐selective catalytic strategy using Ag‐modified chiral Cu electrocatalysts to overcome this intrinsic trade‐off. Structural chirality in the Cu framework induces chirality‐induced spin selectivity, which disfavors spin‐singlet H 2 formation, thereby mitigating the HER and favoring productive hydrogen utilization toward CO 2 hydrogenation. Ag modification facilitates the supply of *CO intermediates on adjacent Cu sites. Thus, the chiral Ag/Cu catalyst selectively drives CO 2 reduction toward CH 4 , delivering a CH 4 Faradaic efficiency (FE) of 67.0% at −0.7 V versus the reversible hydrogen electrode while suppressing the HER. When coupled with perovskite‐based photoelectrochemical electrodes, the chiral catalyst enables unassisted solar‐driven CO 2 ‐to‐CH 4 conversion with an FE CH4 of 54.1% and a solar‐to‐fuel efficiency of 5.86%. These results suggest spin‐selective hydrogen utilization as an effective approach to selective hydrocarbon synthesis and bias‐free solar CO 2 ‐to‐fuel conversion.

title: Breaking the Capacity‐Reversibility Linear Trade‐Off in Li–O 2 Batteries via Amorphous Non‐Precious High‐Entropy Alloy Catalysts
abstract: ABSTRACT Lithium–oxygen (Li–O 2 ) batteries suffer from sluggish reaction kinetics and rely on precious metal‐based catalysts to facilitate the reaction process. Despite being effective, these costly catalysts would inevitably introduce a critical trade‐off between capacity and reversibility, compromising the high energy density advantage of Li–O 2 batteries. In this study, we have designed an amorphous non‐precious MnFeCoNiCu high‐entropy alloy (A‐HEA) catalyst via a mild liquid‐phase reduction strategy to break the above inherent linear trade‐off. The amorphous and porous structure of A‐HEA could provide a large electrochemical active surface area, diluting the local current density to promote the solution‐mediated discharge pathway. This enables the growth of large‐sized Li 2 O 2 to deliver a discharge capacity reaching 10.8 mAh cm −2 . Additionally, the multielemental synergistic electron redistribution of A‐HEA optimizes the d ‐band center to strengthen the LiO 2 adsorption and weaken the O─O bonding, reducing the overpotential to 0.75 V and extending the battery lifetime by 4−5 times compared to the crystalline counterparts. Importantly, the A‐HEA can be produced at a scale of over 100 g and works well in Li–O 2 pouch cells with a rate capability up to 400 mA and an energy density of 754 Wh kg −1 (560 Wh kg −1 even at −30°C).

title: Atomic‐Scale Design, Performance Degradation Mechanisms, and System Integration of Multi‐Principal Element Hydrogen Storage Materials
abstract: ABSTRACT Solid‐state metal hydrides offer high volumetric hydrogen density and intrinsic safety for hydrogen storage, yet their practical application is severely hindered by poor room‐temperature thermodynamics, sluggish kinetics, impurity gas poisoning, difficult activation, and cycling degradation. Multi‐principal element alloys (MPEAs) have recently emerged as promising candidates to overcome these bottlenecks through their vast compositional space, severe lattice distortion, and synergistic cocktail effect. This review systematically summarizes recent advances in MPEAs for solid‐state hydrogen storage, bridging atomic‐scale design to system‐level performance. A unified composition‐process‐structure‐property framework is established that integrates engineering‐driven design rules, post‐processing techniques, multi‐scale computations, machine learning (ML), and high‐throughput experiments. Using advanced in situ and ex situ characterization, the atomic‐scale origins and cross‐scale evolution of surface poisoning, hydrogen‐induced amorphization (HIA), disproportionation, pulverization, and defect accumulation. A theoretical framework linking electronic structure to heat and mass transport is further developed, and hydrogen storage bed design, device integration, fuel‐cell coupling, manufacturing scalability, and cost analysis are discussed. Finally, key scientific and engineering challenges and future research directions are outlined. This review provides scientific guidance for designing MPEA‐based solid‐state hydrogen storage systems with high capacity, long cycle life, high poisoning tolerance, fast de‐/hydrogenation kinetics, and low cost.

title: Engineering High‐Performance Flexible Electronics Through Scalable Manufacturing: Interplay of Materials, Processing, and Morphology
abstract: ABSTRACT Flexible electronics have garnered extensive attention in recent years considering their promising applications across diverse fields such as communications, energy, display, healthcare, and wearable devices. Unlike laboratory‐scale fabrication and integration, the transition of flexible electronics toward commercial applications demands scalable manufacturing that ensures high performance, large‐area reproducibility, high yield, and throughput. However, achieving scalable manufacturing while maintaining device performance remains challenging, as fabrication scale‐up often induces variations in material assembly, morphology evolution, and device integration, which may compromise functional reliability achieved at the laboratory scale. Generally, current flexible electronic devices can be divided into two categories: planar‐type and fiber‐type devices, representing two complementary platforms for realizing large‐scale and highly integrated systems. In this review, scalable fabrication strategies tailored for each category and the latest advances are systematically summarized. In particular, the interplay among material design, scalable processing, morphology evolution, and device integration is highlighted, with emphasis on strategies that preserve device performance during manufacturing scale‐up. Representative planar‐type and fiber‐type flexible electronic systems are further discussed to demonstrate how the synergistic optimization of material design and scalable manufacturing approaches enables high‐performance devices for diverse applications. Finally, we outline remaining challenges and future directions to inform future developments in scalable flexible electronics.

title: Ferroionic‐Assisted, Charge‐Driven Polymorphic Phase Engineering for Multilevel Memristive Devices
abstract: ABSTRACT Memristive device operation can arise from diverse microscopic mechanisms, including charge polarization and trapping, magnetic ordering, ionic migration, and structural phase transitions. Among these, crystalline–crystalline phase transitions in polymorphic materials offer a unique platform for nonvolatile resistance modulation but are often hindered by large energy barriers and limited endurance. Here, we demonstrate a multimodal, charge‐driven phase modulation in an atomically thin polymorphic material, Mo 0.92 W 0.08 Te 2 , enabled by electrostatic coupling to a ferroionic substrate, CuInP 2 S 6 . The polymorphic channel exhibits reversible switching between semiconducting and metallic phases via electrostatically accumulated charges, reflecting the intrinsically low energy barrier between its competing polymorphs. Integration with the ferroionic substrate enables spatially localized, nonvolatile charge accumulation in the channel, which provides distinct, programmable phase‐control pathways under a two‐terminal bias configuration. The phase‐induced resistance modulation through field‐driven ionic processes is governed by the evolution of a phase‐dependent Schottky junction at the electrode–channel interface, yielding multiple, stable conductance states under pulsed electrical excitation. Leveraging these experimentally derived synaptic characteristics, we conducted an MNIST inference simulation with a convolutional neural network, achieving 98.45% accuracy. This ferroionic‐assisted phase‐engineering strategy offers new opportunities beyond traditional phase‐change devices for adaptive electronic and neuromorphic material platforms.

title: Coupling Iodine Conversion and Zinc Ion Transport via Molecular Catalysis for Long‐Life Zinc‐Iodine Batteries
abstract: ABSTRACT Zinc–iodine (Zn–I 2 ) batteries are attractive for low‐cost and scalable energy storage owing to their rapid iodine redox and high theoretical capacity. However, their practical application is severely limited by polyiodide shuttling and interfacial mass‐transport imbalance, where polyiodide immobilization and Zn 2+ accessibility are difficult to reconcile for continuous redox compensation, especially under high‐rate conditions. Here, we address this adsorption–transport conflict by screening a series of metalated tetrakis(4‐carboxyphenyl) porphyrin molecular catalysts and identifying iron (III) meso‐tetrakis (4‐carboxyphenyl) porphyrin (Fe–TCPP) as a unified interfacial regulator catalyst. The Fe–N 4 center provides moderate polyiodide binding, thereby stabilizing iodide intermediates without inducing interfacial passivation. Meanwhile, peripheral carboxyphenyl groups create a zincophilic microenvironment that promotes Zn 2+ accessibility and local ion compensation. This coordinated regulation synchronizes electron transfer and ion redistribution, thereby sustaining reversible iodine redox while avoiding transport blockage. As a result, the Fe–TCPP‐regulated iodine cathode delivers a specific capacity of 178 mAh g −1 and sustains 50 000 cycles at 5 A g −1 . Moreover, a pouch cell with a high iodine loading of 22 mg cm −2 operates stably for more than 1300 cycles. This work establishes a molecular‐catalytic framework for the simultaneous regulation of redox‐intermediate adsorption–conversion and ionic transport in aqueous batteries involving soluble redox species.

Three-way circulation–soil moisture–temperature feedbacks amplify the most extreme mid-latitudinal heat waves
abstract: The most extreme heat waves are intensifying faster than moderate events across many mid-latitude regions. Climate models underestimate these trends, suggesting an incomplete representation and understanding of the underlying physical processes. Here, we use an explainable machine-learning framework to investigate interactions among atmospheric circulation, surface soil moisture, and temperature, and their role in recent heat extremes. We show that a three-way interaction among these components becomes active once a critical temperature threshold is exceeded, contributing, on average, ∼10% to peak temperature anomalies during the most extreme heat events across ∼28% of humid mid-latitude regions. We further reveal that this interaction is systematically underestimated in CMIP6 and CESM2 Large Ensemble simulations. Soils in climate models are too dry at the initiation of heat waves, therefore suppressing subsequent soil-moisture depletion and inhibiting feedback activation. These findings help explain regional model biases in upper-tail warming and highlight avenues for improving future projections of extreme heat events.

title: Measuring mixed-state topological invariant in open photonic quantum walk
abstract: Pure-state manifestations of geometric phase are well established and have found applications across essentially all branches of physics, yet their generalization to mixed-state regimes remains largely unexplored experimentally. The Uhlmann geometric phase offers a natural extension of pure-state paradigms and can exhibit a topological character. However, observation of this invariant is impeded by the incompatibility between Uhlmann parallel transport and Hamiltonian dynamics, as well as the difficulty of preparing topologically nontrivial mixed states. To address this challenge, we report an experimentally accessible protocol for directly measuring the mixed-state topological invariant. By engineering controlled nonunitary dynamics in a photonic quantum walk, we prepare topologically nontrivial mixed states from a trivial initial state. Then, by machine learning the full density matrix in momentum space, we directly extract the quantized geometric phase of the nontrivial mixed states. Furthermore, we observe that this transition of the quantized mixed-state topological invariant from a trivial to a nontrivial value is closely associated with the emergence of a topological kink structure. These results highlight a geometric phase framework that naturally extends to open quantum systems both in and out of thermal equilibrium.

title: Identification of a specialized lipid barrier for Drosophila metamorphosis
abstract: Many terrestrial insects transition from humid to dry environments at metamorphosis, yet how they avoid dehydration is unclear. In Drosophila melanogaster , we identify a lipid barrier to water loss in the pupa that is anatomically distinct from that of the adult. It comprises unisex hydrocarbons that are longer and less volatile than their sex-specific adult counterparts. These hyperlong hydrocarbons are produced by larval oenocytes and stored in the fat body for subsequent transport to the cuticle at pupariation. A fatty acid elongase, EloHL, is required for hyperlong hydrocarbon biosynthesis and for a functional barrier to dehydration during early metamorphosis. Hyperlong barrier hydrocarbons are widespread across the Drosophila genus and typically transition to shorter sex-specific versions during adult maturation. In the desert species D. mojavensis , however, adults retain hyperlong hydrocarbons. This study reveals how insect lipid barriers are tuned to environmental variations in aridity and temperature during development and evolution.

title: Scaling up chemical recycling: High-yield polyolefin pyrolysis to liquid hydrocarbons using iron single atom catalysts
abstract: The chemical recycling of polyolefins (PO) via pyrolysis offers a circular pathway for plastic waste management, yet industrial implementation remains hindered by high energy demands and poor product selectivity. Here, we report an Fe-catalyzed pyrolysis process that achieves 97% PO conversion and a 94% yield of C6 to C35 liquid hydrocarbons. By using a zeolitic imidazolate framework (ZIF)–derived, N-doped porous carbon-supported iron single-atom catalyst (Fe 1 @NC) in combination with a strategic temperature gradient control, we overcome traditional thermolysis limitations. The process was further demonstrated on a kilogram scale, supporting the practical scalability of this catalytic system. Mechanistic investigations reveal that the rate-determining step is an acid base–promoted dehydrogenation of the polymer backbone. Specifically, electronic synergy between the single iron centers and the carbon support stabilizes reactive carbocation intermediates, facilitating their rapid decomposition into high-value olefins and alkanes. These findings provide a scalable and highly efficient catalytic framework for the upcycling of plastic waste into liquid hydrocarbon fractions and chemical feedstocks.

title: Shape-memory scaffold targets inflammation and fibrosis to restore endometrium and fertility in intrauterine adhesions
abstract: Intrauterine adhesion (IUA) is a major cause of infertility, yet current treatments remain limited in preventing fibrosis and restoring functional endometrium. We report a bi-drug, bifunctional, biodegradable shape-memory regenerative (BiSMR) scaffold enabling minimally invasive implantation, sequential drug release, and barrier protection. Proteomic profiling of chemical, mechanical, and combined injury models revealed inflammatory activation, extracellular matrix remodeling, and impaired regenerative programs, providing a molecular rationale for combining epigallocatechin gallate (EGCG) with 17β-estradiol (E 2 ). BiSMR couples an E 2 -loaded PLTG [poly( l -lactide)- co -trimethylene carbonate- co -glycolic acid] backbone with a PDA-EGCG@HAMA coating, enabling rapid EGCG release followed by sustained E 2 delivery. In vitro, BiSMR promoted cell proliferation, migration, angiogenesis, and M2 polarization while suppressing myofibroblast transition. In rat IUA models, BiSMR restored endometrial structure and vascularization, reduced fibrosis, and improved implantation and live birth rates. Proteomics revealed down-regulation of fibrosis- and inflammation-related effectors and restoration of protein biosynthesis and regenerative pathways. BiSMR offers a promising strategy for IUA therapy and fertility restoration.

title: Age reshapes selection on melanoma driver mutations
abstract: Aging is a major risk factor for melanoma. However, it is unclear whether aging fuels tumor evolution by altering mutation rates, changing the microenvironmentally induced selection on drivers, or both. We analyzed 5472 melanomas, estimating how selection on individual variants changes with patient age while accounting for differing neutral mutation rates. Neutral mutation rates increased only modestly with age; ultraviolet damage remained predominant, but endogenous processes increasingly contributed to older tumors. In contrast, selection on major drivers was strongly age dependent: The advantage of BRAF V600E declined precipitously with age, whereas NRAS Q61 mutations gained advantage. TERT promoter mutations became more frequent, yet less advantageous. Aging therefore reshapes melanoma evolution primarily by altering selection, motivating age-conscious evaluation of clinical biomarkers and therapies.

title: Spatial control of enzyme orientation at the lipid droplet interface enables regio- and chemoselective metabolic flux
abstract: Precise spatial control over multienzyme cascade reactions is increasingly recognized as a design lever in synthetic biology for enhancing catalytic performance and directing metabolic flux. By emulating principles of cellular compartmentalization, synthetic scaffolds and engineered interfaces have emerged as powerful platforms to modulate intermediate channeling and reaction efficiency in complex biocatalytic systems. However, robust and spatially defined immobilization of multienzyme assemblies within physicochemically optimal compartments remains challenging because of the dynamic intracellular environment. Here, we reprogram the amphiphilic interface of yeast lipid droplets (LDs) as a programmable scaffold system to support regio- and chemoselective localization of enzymes. Guided by molecular dynamics simulations, we designed LD-anchoring motifs to direct the enzyme orientation at the LD monolayer interface, yielding cytosol-facing or LD inner-facing configurations. Using this designed LD-anchoring motif, we spatially reorganize a trienzyme cascade for prodeoxyviolacein (PDV) biosynthesis across the cytosol-LD interface, facilitating directional conversion of hydrophilic substrates into hydrophobic products. This spatial reorganization substantially improved PDV production by 1300%, achieving 46.25 milligrams per liter. Our approach offers a modular and tunable platform for engineering spatially organized and readily deployable enzyme cascades, opening avenues for biosynthetic catalysis at organellar interfaces.

title: Quantum-interference metrology of dissipative Kerr solitons
abstract: Dissipative Kerr solitons in optical microresonators underpin chip-scale frequency combs with applications ranging from coherent telecommunications to precision spectroscopy. Yet the characterization of their intrinsic femtosecond temporal structure remains challenging, as the low pulse energy and broad spectral bandwidth necessitate optical amplification and careful dispersion compensation in conventional ultrafast diagnostics, both of which can substantial distort the waveform. Here, we demonstrate a quantum-interference metrology of microcomb solitons based on Hong-Ou-Mandel interference. By attenuating the soliton stream to the single-photon level and measuring fourth-order interference, we directly retrieve near transform-limited pulse durations without amplification or dispersion management, remaining accurate even after propagation through 25 kilometers of standard fiber. The same interferogram also provides direct access to the temporal separations in multisoliton states by converting intersoliton separations into additional interference dips at corresponding delays, enabling subpicosecond characterization of their intracavity temporal structure. This quantum-inspired paradigm introduces a metrological approach that is immune to amplification and dispersion distortions, offering a powerful tool for the characterization of complex soliton physics.

title: Temporal dynamics of antigen-specific T cell expansion in primary SARS-CoV-2 infection
abstract: Quantifying T cell response during primary infection in humans is crucial for understanding adaptive immunity. Leveraging a controlled human challenge to severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2, we characterized antigen-specific T cell responses within and across individuals. Notably, individual clones reached similar maximum frequencies despite differences in the timing of their peak expansion. Mathematical modeling within a coarse-grained framework suggested that variability in precursor frequency between different T cell clones could be one mechanism to explain this relationship. Single-cell profiling revealed distinct temporal programs for CD4 + and CD8 + T cells, with CD4 + cells expanding earlier but contracting to a lower frequency. Clones with similar receptors, likely recognizing the same antigen, expanded at similar times. Together, these findings highlight how clone-intrinsic properties such as precursor frequency and CD4/CD8 subset status shape T cell clonal kinetics. These insights provide a quantitative framework for understanding T cell response in humans, with implications for vaccine design.

title: A single–amino acid difference between rodent and human Andes virus affects viral glycoprotein trafficking
abstract: Andes virus (ANDV) causes hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS), with rare outbreaks involving person-to-person transmission. A human ANDV isolate from one such outbreak and a rodent isolate from the same region differ in lethality in Syrian golden hamsters. Genomic analysis revealed 25 nonsynonymous substitutions, including one leading to a T641I change in the human ANDV glycoprotein precursor near its cleavage site. Although the isolates differed in growth kinetics, strand-specific RT-qPCR did not support major differences in viral RNA synthesis, whereas virion release was delayed in the case of the human isolate. In human cell expression systems, a single I641T substitution in the human ANDV glycoprotein resulted in decreased Golgi retention and faster release of virion-like particles relative to wild-type glycoprotein. Since ANDV egress takes place at the Golgi, the T641I change present in the human ANDV isolate may represent a human adaptive mutation influencing glycoprotein trafficking and virus particle release.

title: A transcriptional and cellular exploration of obesity and type II diabetes in human adipose tissues
abstract: Obesity is tightly linked to metabolic disorders such as type II diabetes mellitus (T2D), although a subpopulation of individuals with obesity do not present with these morbidities. The biological factors conferring T2D vulnerability remain incompletely understood. We recruited 58 individuals with obesity with or without a clinical diagnosis of T2D (Ob + T2D and Ob). We profiled paired samples of omental and subcutaneous adipose by single-cell RNA sequencing ( n = 10), flow cytometry under basal and stimulated conditions ( n = 42), and histology ( n = 17). Flow cytometry and chemokine quantification were also performed in paired whole blood. We identified reprogramming of the omental stromal compartment, centered on mesothelial and endothelial cells, alongside contrasting innate T cell and macrophage phenotypes across depots. Mesothelial and IGFBP2 + cells exhibited a fibrotic, epithelial-mesenchymal transition–like phenotype, while omental endothelial cells exhibited a lipid-overload, inflammatory, antigen presentation profile in T2D. Omental and subcutaneous adipose innate T cells exhibited divergent inflammatory profiles between tissues. These findings reveal previously unidentified insights into the pathophysiology of T2D in adipose tissue and identify compensatory networks within the tissues that could be exploited by targeted therapeutics.

title: MYC primes a paralog synthetic lethality involving the mitochondrial translocase subunits TIMM17A and TIMM17B and N-Acetylaspartate
abstract: To identify the genes and pathways required for the survival of MYC -amplified cancers, we engineered an isogenic cell system in which transformation is driven by oncogenic MYC . Using a genome-scale CRISPR-Cas9 library, we identified the mitochondrial membrane translocase TIMM17A as uniquely essential for the survival of MYC-transformed cells. This dependency arises from MYC-driven suppression of TIMM17B , the paralog of TIMM17A . TIMM17A/B is an essential component of the TIM23 mitochondrial protein import complex, and the MYC-induced suppression of TIMM17B creates a strong dependency on TIMM17A . N-acetylaspartate supplementation rescued TIMM17A dependency in MYC -amplified cell lines, highlighting the unique and crucial role of this metabolite in the cell fitness of MYC -amplified cancers. These observations identify a paralog dependency required for the survival of a subset of MYC-driven cancers.

title: The (amide-)N-methylnicotinamide is a microbe-derived NAD + precursor that drives gut stem cell renewal
abstract: Nicotinamide Adenine Dinucleotide (NAD) is a critical cellular coenzyme whose decline associates with various chronic and inflammatory diseases. Improved NAD restoration may reduce disease risks and extend healthy lifespan. We report here that certain commensal bacteria including specific probiotic species produce (amide-)N-methylnicotinamide (N-MNA), which is a structural isomer of methylnicotinamide, a nicotinamide degradative metabolite. Patients with gut dysbiosis and inflammation show reduced stool N-MNA. Stable isotope tracing revealed that N-MNA can be rapidly taken up and incorporated into NAD redox reactions by intestinal epithelial cells (IECs) and non-IECs of fruit fly, mouse, and human. Genetic and pharmacological analyses suggest that N-MNA is converted to NAD + via the Preiss-Handler pathway, independent of the salvage pathway. Cell-type-specific ablation or overexpression of SIRT1, an NAD-consuming enzyme, in Drosophila , along with intestinal stem cell (ISC) lineage tracing in mice revealed that systemic N-MNA supplementation promotes ISC regeneration and gut epithelial repair. Compared to known NAD precursors, N-MNA brings a methyl group into host cells, representing a class of microbe-derived NAD precursor that stimulates the tissue regenerative power.

title: Structure of the Chimalliviridae bacteriophage Goslar reveals host recognition and infection machinery
abstract: Large-genome bacteriophages (phages) of the Chimalliviridae family have a distinctive life cycle, building compartments inside infected bacterial cells that broadly protect their genomes from host defenses. Here, we use cryo–electron microscopy to determine a structure of the Escherichia coli –infecting Chimalliviridae phage Goslar. We combine manual modeling of 25 structural proteins with AlphaFold structure predictions of an additional three proteins to generate a composite model with 2888 protein chains from 28 different structural proteins, totaling more than 1.4 million amino acid residues. Our structure reveals the architecture of the Goslar capsid, portal, tail, and baseplate, highlighting structural similarities and differences with other tailed phages. Combining our structural data with quantitative mass spectrometry of Goslar virions, we identify several high-copy virion-associated proteins that likely play key roles when injected into host cells upon infection. We also identify a Chimalliviridae -specific family of proteins that form long, flexible filaments anchored at the phage baseplate and which incorporate carbohydrate-binding domains, suggesting a key role in host recognition.

title: Prebiotic magnetite enables chirality-magnetic surface feedback
abstract: The emergence of biomolecular homochirality requires both an initial symmetry-breaking event and a mechanism to amplify and preserve a chiral imbalance. Magnetic minerals have been shown to function as chiral agents through the chiral-induced spin selectivity (CISS) effect and may have enabled homochirality on early Earth, yet the magnetic properties of magnetite formed under realistic prebiotic conditions remain unexplored. Here, we show that magnetite synthesized through two geochemically plausible pathways—UV-driven photo-oxidation and nitrite-mediated oxidation of Fe(II)—produces particles dominated by single-vortex and multivortex magnetic domain states. Magnetic measurements and electron microscopy confirm that these populations differ markedly from the nano-fabricated thin-film substrates conventionally used in previous CISS experiments. Using three-dimensional micromagnetic simulations, we demonstrate that single-domain and vortex-state grains undergo irreversible, exchange-driven remagnetization when interacting with spin-polarized homochiral compounds. This magnetic irreversibility provides a robust mechanism for storing and reinforcing weak chiral bias, suggesting that prebiotic magnetite could have contributed to the emergence and stabilization of persistent chiral bias on early Earth.

title: Strigolactone receptor D14 integrates phosphate and strigolactone signaling by interacting with and stabilizing PHR1
abstract: Strigolactone (SL) and low phosphate (LP) signaling coordinately regulate shoot and root architecture and plant adaptation. While LP signaling is generally considered upstream of SL biosynthesis, their interaction is more complex. For instance, exogenous SL exerts opposite effects on lateral root formation under low versus high phosphorus. Here, we show that under LP, SL-induced anthocyanin accumulation requires PHR1, demonstrating that PHR1 functions downstream of SL signaling. We uncovered an SL-dependent physical interaction between PHR1 and the SL receptor DWARF14 (D14). This interaction promotes PHR1 dimerization, stabilizes PHR1 by inhibiting its ubiquitination-mediated degradation, and enhances its transcriptional activation activity. The D14-PHR1 complex directly binds and up-regulates the SL biosynthesis gene MAX3 and anthocyanin biosynthesis genes, thereby inhibiting branching and hypocotyl elongation and promoting anthocyanin accumulation. These findings indicate that PHR1 mediates the coordination of SL and LP signaling, potentially explaining SL’s opposing effects on lateral root formation under different phosphorus conditions. In the phr1 mutant, exogenous SL inhibited lateral roots under both LP and Pi-sufficient conditions, confirming that the promoting role of SL under LP requires PHR1. PHR1 also interacted with D14 to activate LBDs and HB23 , regulating lateral root formation. Collectively, LP signaling coordinates with SL signaling via two parallel pathways: regulating SL biosynthesis to align SL functions with LP requirements and enhancing PHR1 activity through PHR1-D14 interaction to amplify LP signaling outputs.

title: Mevalonate pathway regulates double-negative regulatory T cell stability in metabolic dysfunction–associated steatotic liver disease
abstract: Lipid metabolism dysfunction and immune imbalance are critical pathogenic drivers of metabolic dysfunction–associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD). Double-negative regulatory T cells (DNTreg) are important immune regulatory cells that maintain liver immune homeostasis. However, their survival and function are compromised in MASLD. Herein, we found that mevalonate pathway and its rate-limiting enzyme HMG-CoA reductase (HMGCR) were significantly down-regulated in DNTreg from both mice and patients with MASLD, correlating with impaired DNTreg viability and immunosuppressive function. Arachidonic acid is enriched in MASLD liver and inhibits DNTreg HMGCR expression. Geranylgeranyl pyrophosphate (GGPP), a downstream product of HMGCR, mediates RAC1 geranylgeranylation, which facilitates its interaction with mitochondrial CLPX protease, thereby enhancing mitochondrial function and immunoregulatory activity of DNTreg. Adoptive transfer of Pggt1b +/− DNTreg into MASLD mice demonstrated significantly diminished therapeutic efficacy compared with wild-type DNTreg. In conclusion, mevalonate metabolism–mediated geranylgeranylation is essential for the suppressive activity and immune homeostasis of DNTreg in MASLD.

title: Molecular engineering of noncoordinating backbones in Zr-MOFs for ultrasensitive piezofluorochromism-based high pressure sensing
abstract: Metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) are promising pressure-responsive luminescent materials, but precise control of their emission under pressure remains a substantial challenge. Here, we engineered the piezofluorochromic response of zirconium-based MOFs by tuning the polarity of the emissive moieties through noncoordinating phenyl substituents. Four isostructural UiO-67 derivatives were synthesized. The most polar ligand, in UiO-67-PA, yields ultrasensitive piezofluorochromism with a bathochromic shift of 190 nanometers per gigapascal below 0.36 gigapascals. This sensitivity arises from two cooperative effects: enhanced conjugation through pressure-driven rotation of the aromatic rings and amplified orbital overlap resulting from polarity-induced electronic redistribution. This work broadens the strategies for modulating MOF luminescence and highlights their potential for pressure sensing.

title: Erratum for the Research Article “A combinational chemo-immune therapy using an enzyme-sensitive nanoplatform for dual-drug delivery to specific sites by cascade targeting”
Erratum for the Research Article “CD38-mediated metabolic reprogramming promotes the stability and suppressive function of regulatory T cells in tumor”
Brainstem enkephalinergic neural circuit underlying cold-induced pain relief in mice
abstract: Application of cold or cold-mimicking chemicals to injury has long been recognized as an effective means of pain relief. However, underlying neural mechanisms remain elusive. Here, we identified a cold-responsive neuronal subset within the lateral parabrachial nucleus (lPBN), the thermosensory relay region in the hindbrain, that mediates cold-induced analgesia in mice. Activation of these neurons and their projection to ventrolateral periaqueductal gray (vlPAG) increased the nociceptive threshold, while ablation of these neurons attenuated analgesia induced by cold-mimicking chemicals. We further identified that these neurons express precursor gene of enkephalin ( Penk ), which is necessary for TRPM8 (transient receptor potential melastatin 8)–mediated pain relief. Mechanistically, cold-responsive lPBN neurons frequency-dependently released enkephalin peptide into vlPAG to activate the descending pain modulation circuitry via disinhibition. Activation of cold-responsive neurons reduced spinal cord responses to noxious stimuli, suggesting the involvement of a top-down pain modulation pathway. These findings propose a central mechanism underlying cold-induced pain relief, which could be a novel therapeutic target.

title: Y chromosome instability in the early mouse embryo
abstract: The Y chromosome lacks canonical centromeric repeats necessary for high-fidelity chromosome segregation. In adult tissues, this causes Y loss and predisposes to disease. However, its impact on embryogenesis is unknown. Here, we identify the first mouse embryonic mitoses as a window during which the Y centromere is unusually weak. This vulnerability impairs kinetochore strength and the Y becomes preferentially trapped at the spindle pole, resulting in missegregation. To study the impact of Y loss, we generate an aggregation model to track specific aneuploidies in mosaic embryos. Loss of the Y slows down cell division and compromises embryo size. Our findings reveal a developmental window during which the Y is especially vulnerable to loss, with implications for male sex determination and the origin of Turner syndrome (XO).

title: Humid periods over western Sahara during the Middle Miocene Climate Transition and their implications on the carbon cycle
abstract: The Middle Miocene expansion of the Antarctic Ice Sheet coincides with major sedimentological changes in Malta. This interval also saw reorganisations in ocean circulation linked to closure of the Mesopotamian Seaway (MSR-events) and perturbations in the carbon cycle (CM events). The final CM event (CM-6), slightly lags the main glacial phase and remains difficult to interpret due to competing mechanisms and conflicting p CO 2 reconstructions. To explore links between cryosphere, circulation, hydroclimate, and the carbon cycle, we present new geochemical records from Malta. Our records show that cryospheric expansion was followed by large, precessionally paced variations in sea-surface salinity and a marked regional increase in biological productivity. The results indicate a shift toward stronger monsoonal influence, delivering enhanced freshwater and nutrient fluxes to the region. This enhanced local biological carbon pump may have acted as a positive feedback to a global CO 2 drawdown. However, any contribution to global CO 2 drawdown remains tentative and cannot be confirmed without contemporaneous high-resolution open-ocean records.

title: Visualizing nanoscopic acoustic mode competition in a van der Waals ferroelectric
abstract: Understanding how low-dimensional ferroelectrics respond to ultrafast excitation at nanoscales is essential for controlling energy flow and mechanical functionality in next-generation polar devices, yet the nanoscopic structural response to ultrafast depolarization remains unresolved, obscuring the microscopic pathways of acoustic decoherence and energy dissipation. Here, we spatiotemporally resolve lattice motion in the van der Waals ferroelectric NbOI 2 using combined ultrafast electron microscopy and diffraction, revealing three acoustic phonons: two transverse shear modes and one longitudinal breathing mode. The transverse mode that shears the layers perpendicular to the in-plane polar axis dominates over that along the polar axis, reflecting anisotropic polarization-strain coupling. Real-space mapping uncovers spatially correlated heterogeneity in mode amplitudes and lifetimes. Regions dominated by a single shear mode exhibit significantly longer acoustic lifetimes than multimode regions, suggesting acoustic phonon–phonon scattering as a major source of decoherence. Our results provide a microscopic understanding of ultrafast depolarization-driven acoustic dynamics and spatially heterogeneous energy dissipation in van der Waals ferroelectrics.

title: Explainable AI identifies recombination and chromatin environment as key predictors of subgenome evolution in maize and Brassica
abstract: Polyploidy, or whole genome duplication, reshapes genomes through biased gene loss and regulatory rewiring, yet the drivers of biased fractionation among subgenomes remain unclear. Using maize and Brassica rapa as model allopolyploids, we compiled 60 genomic and epigenomic features in maize and 45 in B. rapa and constructed supervised machine learning models to classify genes by subgenome identity. In both species, eXplainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) approaches identified recombination rate as the most influential and highly interconnected feature despite nonsignificant mean differences between subgenome groups. Chromosome location, transposon density, and chromatin-associated features, including the proximity of accessible chromatin regions to genes and active histone marks such as H3K9ac and H3K27ac, consistently ranked among the top contributors to subgenome classification. XAI-derived covariation and interaction networks further revealed recombination rate as the central node connecting significant features. Together, these results highlight recombination and chromatin environment as major predictors of subgenome divergence in polyploid genomes.

title: Dual-acting compounds that deliver an acidifying domain via zanamivir to the virus surface are potent influenza inhibitors
abstract: While contemporary antiviral development primarily strives to produce “lock and key” inhibitors, we present here a different approach to drug design that uses compounds devised to alter the microenvironment of the virion surface, making it incompatible with virus entry. We illustrate this strategy with inhibitors of influenza virus and show that compounds designed to produce a proton-rich mantle above the virion surface affect the ability of the viral hemagglutinin to interact with cellular receptors and gain entry to the cell. The compounds show exceptional antiviral activity both in vitro and in vivo and protect against influenza illness in ferrets and in mice after a single dose, either therapeutically or prophylactically.

title: Ultrafast Meissner-levitated microrotor
abstract: Levitated mechanical systems offer a powerful and flexible platform for the realization of ultralow-noise sensors and tests of fundamental physics. Here, we report the demonstration of a levitated microrotor, consisting of a magnetic microsphere levitated by the Meissner effect at 4.2 kelvin. The rotor reaches rotation frequencies above 2.3 megahertz (138 million revolutions per minute) while exhibiting an exceptionally low damping rate of 4.75 × 10 −7 hertz. Exploiting the linear dependence of friction on the gas density, we demonstrate high-accuracy absolute pressure sensing over a wide range at cryogenic temperature. Last, we detect the thermal torque noise at intermediate pressure by operating the rotor in synchronized mode, resulting in a first preliminary narrowband search for axion-like dark matter. More broadly, the combination of high rotational speed, low temperature, and low thermal torque noise establishes a previously unidentified regime for precision measurements, with direct implications for the detection of extremely weak forces and fields.

title: CD8 + T cells induce RIPK1-regulated brain endothelial cell death in cerebral malaria
abstract: Cerebral malaria (CM) is a potentially lethal complication of Plasmodium falciparum infection characterized by blood-brain barrier disruption and brain hemorrhage. Although immune-mediated endothelial damage is central to CM pathology, the mechanisms linking cytotoxic immune responses to endothelial injury remain unclear. Here, we show that CD8 + T cells induce receptor-interacting serine/threonine-protein kinase 1 (RIPK1)–regulated cell death of brain endothelial cells in mouse CM, while RIPK1 phosphorylation is increased in brain endothelial cells in human CM. Using magnetic resonance imaging, three-dimensional tissue-cleared brain imaging, cross-species pathology, endothelial translatomics, immunocerebrovascular interactomics, and genetic association testing, we identify a CD8 + T cell–dependent, RIPK1-centered mouse endothelial cell death program. Combined RIPK1 and caspase inhibition protected cross-presenting endothelial cells from CD8 + T cell–mediated death in vitro. In vivo, brain endothelial-specific genetic inactivation or systemic pharmacological inhibition of RIPK1 kinase activity prolonged survival in mouse CM without altering parasitemia. These findings support RIPK1 inhibition as a promising therapeutic strategy to counter CD8 + T cell–induced endothelial death in CM.

title: A full-hardware edge detection system based on a highly robust dual random number generator
abstract: Conventional edge computing hardware at autonomous driving terminals is limited by chip area and power efficiency for complex image data. Recently, researchers have used memristors to construct dedicated hardware systems, achieving advancements in multiple image processing fields such as pattern recognition and edge detection. However, a full-hardware image processing system with anti-interference, low power, and high real-time performance remains challenging. Here, we fabricated a volatile Ag/AlO x /n-Si memristor with exceptional stability and low power. High-resolution electron microscopy visualized Ag conductive filament formation. Integrating two memristors with a logic circuit, we designed a low-power edge detection unit using dual random number hardware computation. Its energy consumption is 92.3% lower than traditional logic circuits, with strong anti-interference. To validate practical use, we constructed a 32-channel parallel full-hardware system with 64 devices, achieving 31.25 frames per second and excellent edge detection. The system exhibits excellent scalability, stability, and anti-interference, offering great potential for edge vision hardware in autonomous driving, safety monitoring, and surgical assistance.

title: A robust spin-coupled tetraradical via nonalternant design
abstract: Polyradicals in open-shell polycyclic hydrocarbons (PHs) offer access to multiple spin states and hold great promise for spintronics and quantum technologies. Here we report a nonalternant, air-stable tetraradical featuring two fused 7-5-7 rings and a strongly correlated singlet ground state. This molecule displays an exceptional tetraradical character ( y 0 = 1.00, y 1 = 0.89) and exhibits long ambient stability ( t 1/2 = 33 days). Comprehensive electronic structure and magnetic response analyses reveal that the spin topology is governed by both ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic interactions, with robust electron correlation ( J 1 = +321 K, J 2 = −44 K, and J 3 = −29 K). The unique nonalternant design suppresses hyperfine and vibrational decoherence, giving rise to long spin relaxation and coherence time. These findings demonstrate that embedding nonalternant motifs into PH polyradicals provides a powerful strategy to simultaneously promote molecular stability, spin-exchange coupling, and spin robustness—key features for materials in the rising field of quantum information science.

title: Photonic entanglement swapping with remote quantum dots
abstract: Entanglement swapping is a protocol that details how to create entanglement between previously uncorrelated particles. Its photonic version, mediated by the interference of photon pairs generated by separate quantum systems, finds disparate applications in quantum networks. So far, entanglement swapping with entangled photons from remote systems has been implemented only using probabilistic sources. However, the scaling up of quantum networks requires nonprobabilistic quantum emitters without a trade-off between the degree of entanglement and photon-pair generation rate. Here, we demonstrate photonic entanglement swapping using photon pairs generated by two separate GaAs quantum dots. The emitters are deterministically embedded in hybrid semiconductor-piezoelectric devices that make the entangled photons from two dissimilar quantum dots nearly identical. Entanglement swapping is demonstrated with a fidelity as high as 0.71(2), more than 10 SDs above the classical limit. The experimental data are quantitatively explained by a theoretical model that also suggests how to boost the protocol performance. Our work opens the path to the exploitation of quantum dot entangled-photon sources in quantum repeater networks.

title: High-impulse and reactant-regenerative combustion-based micro actuators
abstract: The use of combustibles in micro-actuator technologies enables powerful impulsive actuation capabilities comparable to those of natural organisms. However, the exogenous dependence of fuel limits the development of combustion-based actuators. We present a closed-cycle reactant regeneration strategy wherein the bidirectional interconversion between hydrogen and water achieves real-time fuel replenishment for reactant-regenerative electrolysis and combustion reactions. Based on this, we develop a 1.5-centimeter actuator that generates forces above 20 newtons and operates continuously for >7200 cycles without refueling (a two orders-of-magnitude improvement over existing combustion-based actuators). Experiments confirm its strength and cross-environment versatility for removing obstacles, jetting, and striking via underwater cavitation. These features enable the actuator to be integrated into small robotic platforms, allowing them to reconfigure local surroundings in an active manner.

title: Pink noise in dyads’ semantic similarity trajectories predicts conversation enjoyment
abstract: Conversation is a core component of human social life. Many influential theories treat conversation as a linear system, i.e., the sum of its parts. However, linear accounts of semantic entrainment lose explanatory power at their upper limits: Discussing perfectly aligned opinions becomes boring. We propose an alternate account that considers the multiscale organization of semantic similarity over the course of a conversation, as indexed by pink noise. Here, we test whether pink noise can be found in interlocutors’ conavigated trajectories through semantic space. Not only is pink noise present, but its strength predicts positive conversation outcomes like enjoyment and connection, increases with practice, and is reflected in a large language model’s representation of conversation quality. These results demonstrate an important role for scale-free dynamics in characterizing successful conversation.

title: Revisiting the additionality and durability of carbon uptake in large-scale ocean iron fertilization
abstract: Climate stabilization pathways limiting global warming to 1.5° to 2°C require rapid emission reductions alongside additional carbon dioxide removal (CDR) of ∼2 to 3 PgC year −1 . Our simulations show that sustained century-scale ocean iron fertilization (OIF) in the southern sector of the Southern Ocean (SSO) provides a contribution of ∼30 PgC, equivalent to ∼0.3 PgC year −1 . This uptake nearly matches the additional carbon uptake from global fertilization. In other iron-limited regions, fertilization-induced uptake is largely offset (70 to 100%) by anomalous outgassing in nonfertilized regions. After terminating OIF following 30 years of fertilization, the ocean retains ∼50% of the additional carbon in the SSO, whereas retention is negligible elsewhere. These results identify the SSO as the most favorable region for durable carbon removal through large-scale OIF, particularly in terms of additionality and durability, although its carbon uptake is smaller than earlier estimates. OIF-induced CDR is constrained by local and remote nutrient depletion, carbon reentrainment, incomplete macronutrient drawdown, and reduced phytoplankton carbon-to-phosphorus ratios. Incomplete macronutrient drawdown reflects the uptake controls by light, top-down controls, and rates of macronutrient resupply. Further insight into OIF potential will be enabled by standardized multimodel comparisons and targeted analysis of nutrient drawdown controls.

title: Combating drug-resistant Aeromonas veronii : Multiomics revealed the antibacterial mechanism of resveratrol
abstract: Aeromonas , widely distributed in aquatic ecosystems, is a prevalent fish pathogen and can cause human infections via contaminated aquatic products, polluted water contact, or tainted food consumption. Escalating antibiotic resistance in Aeromonas strains highlights an urgent need for alternative natural antimicrobial agents. This study investigated resveratrol’s antibacterial mechanisms against Aeromonas veronii and evaluated its protective efficacy in hybrid sturgeon. Resveratrol exhibited strong activity [minimum inhibitory concentration: 128 microgram per milliliter (μg/ml), minimum bactericidal concentration: 256 μg/ml], disrupting cell wall/membrane integrity, inducing reactive oxygen species accumulation, inhibiting adenosine 5′-triphosphate synthesis, and down-regulating key metabolic pathways via transcriptomic and metabolomic analyses. In the sturgeon infection model, resveratrol-nanoemulsion notably improved survival, reduced tissue bacterial loads, mitigated oxidative stress and inflammation, and restored intestinal barrier function. These findings confirm resveratrol as a promising antibiotic alternative against A. veronii , with nanoemulsion formulation enhancing its therapeutic efficacy.

title: Adaptive dual-programming magnetic soft robot with lifelike behavior
abstract: Magnetic soft robots with embodied intelligence of multimodal motions, environmental perception, and functional decoupling depend on ingenious material arrangement and programmable morphing information introduction. While some efforts have been made, achieving lifelike behaviors for soft robots in system-level strategy remains a notable challenge. Here, we present dual-programming hydrogel-based soft robots (DHSRs) that couple magnetic and anisotropic programming through the spatial arrangement of patterned magnetic skeletons into responsive and structural hydrogel bodies. These DHSRs exhibit programmable exquisite and multicurved structures in three-dimensional (3D) space, environment-adaptive deformation behaviors proved by switching from random jumping on land to regular swimming in water of a fish-like soft robot, and further locomotion-function decoupling capabilities of region-selective cargo delivery in an integrated “locomotion-perception-action” workflow. Our strategy in biomedical potential is exemplified by a ring-like pH-responsive DHSR for gastric ulcer therapy, which integrates multimodal locomotion (rolling, tumbling, and rotating), adaptive matching, and microneedle-mediated penetration. By collaborating with a capsule endoscopy system, we explore the possibility of a wireless and painless diagnostic-therapeutic platform in a pig model. This strategy endows the robot with perception and multitask execution capabilities, highlighting a promising route for the intelligent evolution of soft robots across diverse application domains.

title: Electron competition in azobenzene programs infection-adaptive antibacterial therapy
abstract: Conventional stimulus-responsive antibacterial systems generally operate through binary trigger–activation mechanisms, making them poorly suited to evolving infection microenvironments and thereby contributing to persistent infection and resistance development. Here, we establish an azobenzene-based kinetic regulatory system in which oxygen gradients commonly present in infected tissues continuously program reaction kinetics through electron competition. Oxygen acts as a competing electron acceptor within the reductive reaction network, partitioning electron transfer between azo reduction and oxygen consumption. Substituent electronic structures further reshape reduction propensity, encoding distinct kinetic behaviors. These electronically programmed kinetics translated into adaptive nanoscale dissociation and drug-release profiles: Electron-rich azobenzenes rapidly disassembled under severe hypoxia, whereas electron-withdrawing structures sustained release under mild hypoxia, generating infection state–adaptive antibacterial outputs. Moreover, the same electronic features governing reduction kinetics also reduced the reactivity and toxicity of reductive metabolites. This work establishes electron competition as a strategy for converting environmental gradients into continuous kinetic outputs for adaptive antibacterial therapy.

title: Comprehensive degron mapping in human transcription factors
abstract: Gene expression is regulated by the targeted degradation of transcription factors through the ubiquitin-proteasome system. Transcription factors destined for degradation are recognized by E3 ubiquitin-protein ligases through motifs termed degrons, embedded within the sequence. In this study, we systematically map degrons in all 1626 human transcription factors. We find thousands of both known and previously unidentified degrons and characterize their sequence properties. Active degrons placed within exposed and intrinsically disordered regions contribute to modulating the abundance of the transcription factors, while the most common somatic mutations that are linked to skin cutaneous melanoma lead to unfolding and exposure of a latent degron buried in the zinc finger structure. We present examples of compartment-specific degrons and demonstrate that variant effects in transcription factors correlate with degron potency. Last, we show that while >60% of all predicted transcriptional activation domains overlap with strong degrons, acidic residues within the remaining transactivating regions counter the degron potency, showing how degrons can shape the transcription factor sequence landscape.

title: Reciprocal control of genome instability and RNA processing in cancer: Mechanisms and therapeutic opportunities
abstract: Genomic instability and dysregulated RNA processing are each recognized as core hallmarks of cancer, but accumulating evidence indicates that they are mechanistically intertwined rather than independent features. Chromosomal instability, mismatch-repair deficiency, and homologous recombination deficiency can reshape RNA splicing, 3′ end formation, and RNA surveillance through changes in gene dosage, DNA damage signaling, and alterations in regulatory elements. Conversely, aberrant splicing, polyadenylation, and RNA modifications can impair DNA repair, perturb mitotic control, and promote replication stress, thereby reinforcing genomic instability. This bidirectional circuit drives clinically relevant phenotypes, including therapeutic resistance, immune modulation, and emergent vulnerabilities that are not captured by DNA-centric biomarkers alone. Here, we present a unified framework for the genome instability–RNA processing axis and its direct clinical implications for cancer diagnosis, treatment stratification, and therapeutic exploitation, highlighting the most actionable mechanistic interfaces and discussing how integrated DNA-RNA biomarkers and rational combination strategies could extend precision oncology beyond static genomic lesions.

title: Spatial proteomics reveals lipid droplet reorganization in symbiotic Paramecium bursaria cells
abstract: Endosymbiosis is an important adaptive mechanism allowing organisms to exploit previously inaccessible niches. The flexible relationship between the ciliate Paramecium bursaria and green algae represents a model system for studying early endosymbiosis evolution. However, the mechanisms underlying how P. bursaria cells maintain this endosymbiotic relationship remain unclear. Here, we use mass spectrometry–based proteomics to generate a spatial proteomic atlas of the host P. bursaria cells with and without endosymbionts. This atlas defines the protein composition of the endosymbiont-containing compartment (perialgal vacuole) and reveals pronounced remodeling of host lipid droplets upon symbiosis. Imaging analyses confirm that lipid droplets change in size, morphology, and positioning, accumulating near intracellular algae. Perturbing symbiotic cells with chemical inhibitors of lipid metabolism reduces endosymbiotic algal numbers, revealing a role for lipid droplets in the host-endosymbiont interaction. Our data provide a comprehensive resource for protein localization in P. bursaria cells and elucidate how those cells remodel an existing cellular compartment to maintain endosymbiosis.
